divergences.other_says: Study conducted by a joint English-Portuguese research group

divergences.en_says: Not mentioned specifically; only notes it was long considered synonym of Apatosaurus for decades
divergences.other_says: States specifically that in 1903 B. excelsus was reclassified as A. excelsus

divergences.other_says: States researchers in 2015 proposed three species: B. excelsus, B. yahnahpin, and B. parvus, without individual dates

divergences.other_says: States adults estimated up to 15 tons and up to 22 meters long, without species distinction
divergences.evidence_en: largest species B. excelsus reaching up to 21–23 m (69–75 ft)... and weighing in at 15–20 t

divergences.en_says: Detailed classification within Diplodocidae family and Apatosaurinae subfamily, including 1929 naming and 2015 validation
divergences.other_says: IT and MK do not mention Diplodocidae or Apatosaurinae subfamily classification at all
divergences.evidence_en: Brontosaurus is a genus in the subfamily Apatosaurinae, which includes only it and Apatosaurus

summary: The EN Wikipedia lead is the most detailed, including specific paleontological attribution (Tschopp et al.), precise geographic and stratigraphic data, detailed size estimates per species, and taxonomic classification within Diplodocidae/Apatosaurinae. The IT edition attributes the 2015 reclassification study to an England-Portugal research group rather than naming Tschopp, and adds historical detail about the 1903 reclassification not found in EN. The MK edition (largely garbled with template code) offers a more generalized, less precise account, omitting specific dates, locations narrowed to Utah/Wyoming, and detailed taxonomic subfamily discussion, while giving broader size and geographic claims lacking species-level distinction found in EN.
